name: KTTKS

lead: KTTKS is a five-amino-acid peptide, usually attached to a palmitoyl fat chain (Pal-KTTKS) and sold as Matrixyl in anti-wrinkle products since 2000. People use it to smooth fine lines and firm skin.

It is a matrikine, a messenger peptide reported to stimulate extracellular matrix and collagen synthesis in skin cells, and the fat chain is meant to aid penetration. A 12-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled split-face study of 93 women aged 35 to 55 assessed it in photoaged facial skin and reported improvement, and lab work shows it raises collagen production in cultured fibroblasts. Reviewers discuss how well the peptide reaches the dermis.

paras: It is used as a leave-on serum or cream ingredient, typically as part of a daily anti-aging routine. Studies of it ran for around 12 weeks.
The sources reviewed do not report safety problems. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.

angle.text: KTTKS, sold as Matrixyl in palmitoylated form, is a collagen-signalling peptide used in anti-wrinkle skincare. It signals skin cells to make more collagen and matrix, which smooths fine lines. A 93-subject split-face trial studied it, and skin penetration is discussed in the literature.

lead: KTTKS is a pentapeptide (lysine-threonine-threonine-lysine-serine) used in anti-wrinkle skin care, usually in its palmitoylated form, palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Pal-KTTKS), sold under the trade name Matrixyl. Sederma launched Matrixyl in 2000. It is classed as a matrikine, a messenger peptide that regulates cell activity [1][2][3].

People use it in serums and creams in the hope of visibly softer lines and firmer-looking skin: the idea is that the peptide signals skin cells to make more collagen and other matrix components, so photoaged skin looks smoother over weeks of use [4][3]. In a 12-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled, split-face study of 93 women aged 35 to 55, a moisturiser containing 3 ppm pal-KTTKS was compared with the same moisturiser without it, and the authors reported significant improvement in wrinkles and fine lines by technical and expert-grader image analysis [5]. Laboratory work shows C16-KTTKS stimulates collagen production in human fibroblasts [4]. Whether enough peptide reaches the dermis is discussed in the literature [3][6][7].

The peptide is one of the most widely known cosmetic peptides and is mentioned in forums that discuss skin-focused looksmaxxing, where members compare it with the copper peptide GHK-Cu [8][9]. It is regulated as a cosmetic ingredient in most jurisdictions [10].
infobox: Fragment of the type I procollagen C-terminal propeptide [11]
Cosmetic ingredient (some peptides are prescription medicines in Australia and New Zealand)

paras: The KTTKS sequence is a fragment of the C-terminal propeptide of type I procollagen. A peptide-industry profile credits Kazuhiro Katayama and colleagues, in the early 1990s, with identifying it as the smallest segment that stimulates extracellular matrix production in fibroblasts [11]. The matrikine concept, in which fragments of matrix proteins act as signals to cells, was set out by Maquart and co-workers and is cited by Wikipedia as the origin of the idea [1][10].

Sederma, a French cosmetic-ingredient maker, attached a 16-carbon palmitoyl chain to the peptide to make it more lipophilic; the same profile credits Karl Lintner with leading that work, reports patent filings in 1999 and describes the launch of Matrixyl in 2000 [11][1]. A 2006 Dermatology Times article reported that researchers at the University of Tennessee had shown a pentapeptide raising collagen I production in fibroblast culture, that Procter & Gamble had licensed it and that Sederma held the patent [12]. Before 2006 the ingredient was listed as palmitoyl pentapeptide-3; its name then changed to palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 [1].

Later Sederma products carry related names but are different ingredients. Matrixyl 3000 combines palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7, and Matrixyl Synthe'6 is a palmitoylated hexapeptide (palmitoyl tripeptide-38), according to the peptide-industry profile [11]. Wikipedia lists KPV tripeptide, GHK-Cu, glycyl-prolyl-hydroxyproline and palmitoyl tripeptide-38 as related cosmetic peptides [1].

Pal-KTTKS has the formula C39H75N7O10 and a molar mass of about 802 g/mol; it consists of five amino acids attached to a palmitic acid chain [1]. The fatty chain is meant to help the molecule pass through the lipid structures of the skin [1][2]. The palmitoylated molecule is a peptide amphiphile: studies show C16-KTTKS self-assembles into nanotape structures in water and that this self-assembly relates to its collagen-stimulating activity in cell culture [4]. Researchers have also made liposome-encapsulated and ionic-liquid-conjugated versions to improve stability or delivery [13][14].

KTTKS is a cosmetic ingredient aimed at wrinkles and photoaged skin, found in serums, creams and eye products [1][3]. Wikipedia lists the claimed effect as an anti-wrinkle effect and cites in vitro and in vivo studies, some by the manufacturer and some by independent groups [2]. Experimental work has also examined the peptide in wound contraction and, in animal models, in dressings for burns [2][15].

Consumer products vary in how the ingredient is named and how much is present. The peptide-industry profile reports typical concentrations of about 2 to 8 percent of a premixed solution, notes that labels such as '10% Matrixyl' may refer to a premix whose pal-KTTKS content is far lower, and says results in the cited trials took 8 to 12 weeks [11].

Matrikines are peptides that signal cells through specific receptors; Wikipedia describes the peptide as activating genes involved in extracellular matrix renewal and cell proliferation, a statement the page itself flags as needing a medical citation [1][10]. In vitro, C16-KTTKS stimulated collagen production in human dermal and corneal fibroblasts in a concentration-dependent manner [4]. A 2011 review found a sound in vitro basis for an effect on fibroblasts, with specific stimulation of collagen types I and III and fibronectin expression [3]. Related work found KTTKS increased type I collagen and TGF-beta expression in tendon cells [16]. A review of cosmetic genomics lists Pal-KTTKS among compounds whose biological effects were characterised through gene-expression profiling [17].

Peptides are large, mostly hydrophilic molecules, which makes delivery into skin difficult. A 2022 review concluded that most anti-wrinkle peptides need permeation-enhancement strategies to reach their targets [6]. The 2011 KTTKS review noted a surprising absence of in vitro skin-penetration data and relatively few clinical studies [3]. A 2014 study measured the stability and permeation of KTTKS and pal-KTTKS in hairless mouse skin [7], and another examined microneedle-enhanced delivery of cosmeceutical peptides in human skin [18]. At the time of the 2006 Dermatology Times piece, dermatologist Zoe Draelos said that to 'reprogram collagen, they need to get to the dermis and penetrate the stratum corneum' [12]. Manufacturer and independent investigators therefore differ in emphasis: the palmitoyl chain is described by the maker as the penetration aid, while reviewers describe the question as open [1][3][6].

The best-known study is the 12-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled, split-face, left-right randomised trial in 93 Caucasian women aged 35 to 55 who applied a moisturiser alone to one side and the same moisturiser with 3 ppm pal-KTTKS to the other. The authors reported that the peptide was well tolerated and gave significant improvement versus control in wrinkles and fine lines by both technical and expert-grader analysis, and subjects' self-assessments also showed improvement [5]. The study is by Robinson and colleagues, 2005 [1].

A 2009 pair of double-blind, randomised split-face studies (42 and 35 women aged 30 to 70) tested several moisturising products over four weeks and measured crow's-feet roughness by 3-D imaging; the products contained niacinamide, the peptides Pal-KT and Pal-KTTKS and carnosine, and several significantly improved smoothness relative to no treatment [19]. Because the tested products combined several actives, the studies assess the formulations rather than a single peptide.

A 2011 review of topical KTTKS described few clinical studies [3]. The peptide-industry profile adds that much of the available data is industry-sourced, and cites a four-month comparison against retinol in which both raised skin thickness by a similar amount, with pal-KTTKS acting earlier and causing less irritation [11]. A related tetrapeptide, GEKG, was designed from the same matrikine concept and reported to reduce roughness in a placebo-controlled study of 30 volunteers [20].

In the 93-woman study the peptide was reported as well tolerated [5]. The peptide-industry profile says the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel concluded the ingredient is safe as used in cosmetics, that reported irritation usually traces to other formulation ingredients, and that data on pregnancy and lactation are limited [11]. Wikipedia's page on matrikines notes that some peptides show pro-ageing effects and that, at high doses, others may promote tumour growth, as general statements about the class [10].

Matrixyl and related peptides are marketed in cosmetic products as anti-wrinkle actives, and are used in 'peptide serums' sold through mainstream and direct-to-consumer brands [1][10]. Most matrikines are used mainly in cosmetics, and some regulators, including those in Australia and New Zealand, class certain peptides as prescription medicines while most of the world treats them as cosmetics [10]. In the 2006 Dermatology Times article, Draelos described peptides as the newest realm in cosmeceuticals and expected many more products [12].

In skin-focused looksmaxxing discussion, KTTKS is mentioned as a topical collagen-support option. One looksmax.org thread has a member weighing topical GHK-Cu against Matrixyl after seeing Matrixyl recommended in another member's skin looksmaxxing thread, with the original poster saying they have 'pretty much the same effect', and a first reply answering 'ghk-cu' [8]. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article lists topical GHK-Cu among softmaxxing practices and says studies have linked it to improved skin tightness and fewer wrinkles [9].

GHK-Cu, glycyl-prolyl-hydroxyproline and palmitoyl tripeptide-38 are listed as related cosmetic peptides [1]. Acetyl hexapeptide-3 (marketed as 'botulinum-like') and hexapeptide-10 are other matrikine-class or signal peptides in cosmetics [10]. Dermatologists have described some of these, including the neuromodulator-style peptides, as possibly acting more like moisturisers than true neuromuscular agents [12]. Retinoids, the standard evidence-backed topical for photoageing, are described separately in dermatology references.

timeline.event: Early 1990s: Katayama and colleagues identify KTTKS, a procollagen I propeptide fragment, as stimulating extracellular matrix production in fibroblasts (date given only approximately) [11].
Sederma files patents on palmitoylated peptides [11].
Sederma launches Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide) as a cosmetic active [1].
Robinson and colleagues report the 12-week split-face study of pal-KTTKS in 93 women [5][1].
The INCI name changes from palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 to palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 [1].
Split-face studies of peptide-containing products on crow's feet are published [19].
A review of topically applied KTTKS notes limited clinical and penetration data [3].
C16-KTTKS shown to stimulate collagen production in human fibroblasts [4].
Stability and permeation of KTTKS and pal-KTTKS studied in hairless mouse skin [7].
A review examines skin permeability as a requirement for anti-wrinkle peptide performance [6].
